ADR-0001.title: T1 automated gate holds via CI or pre-commit hook — never via discipline
ADR-0001.truth_callout: ⚠️ CURRENT TRUTH: the core principle still holds — an automated gate via CI or pre-commit hook, never discipline. Revoked: the "has remote → CI" dispatch (which installed a GitHub workflow on any host). Current rule: dispatch by remote host — see ADR-0006.
ADR-0001.body:
# T1 automated gate holds via CI or pre-commit hook — never via discipline

## Context and Problem

STANDARD §3 originally defined T1 as "everything in this document, with `docs-check` in CI". The pilot repository (console-platon) has no git remote — making CI impossible — so the adopting agent improvised by placing `docs-check` in the router's global DoD. That is a documentation-only gate: it only runs if someone remembers to run it. Under the standard's design criterion ("complexity sustained by human discipline rots"), a T1 repository without an automated gate is T1 in name only.

## Decision Drivers

- Standard design criterion: tool-enforced validation, never human discipline.
- Offline/local repositories are a real use case (the pilot itself), not a theoretical edge case.
- The gate must execute without relying on human memory or external infrastructure.

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Keep CI mandatory

**Pros:** unbypassable gate at merge time; zero ambiguity.

**Cons:** a repository without a remote is formally excluded from T1, inviting false tier declarations.

### Option 2 — Accept the router's DoD as the gate

**Pros:** zero setup cost.

**Cons:** pure discipline without automated enforcement — the exact failure mode the standard forbids.

### Option 3 — Pre-commit hook as an equivalent local gate

**Pros:** real automation without a remote; runs on every commit; single-line installation.

**Cons:** bypassable via `--no-verify`; installed per clone (git does not version hooks).

## Decision

Option 3. T1 requires `docs-check` in an **automated gate**: CI when a remote exists; a **pre-commit hook** when there is no remote. The reference repository provides both adapters (`.github/workflows/docs-check.yml` and `scripts/pre-commit`). Bypassing via `--no-verify` is accepted: it is a deliberate, visible act rather than forgetfulness.

## Consequences

- A repository without a remote can legitimately operate at T1.
- Once the repository gains a remote, CI takes over and the hook becomes cheap redundancy (preserving fast local feedback).
- For adopters: install the hook during adoption (§10) whenever CI is absent.
- STANDARD §2, §3, §8, and §10 updated in the same commit that accepts this ADR.

## Confirmation

```bash
test -f .github/workflows/docs-check.yml || grep -q docs-check .git/hooks/pre-commit   # exit 0: a gate exists
```

## Notes

Lesson learned from the console-platon pilot (adoption on 2026-06-09).

ADR-0002.title: Pending items and NNNN reservations live in docs/BACKLOG.md when there is no issue tracker
ADR-0002.body:
# Pending items and NNNN reservations live in docs/BACKLOG.md when there is no issue tracker

## Context and Problem

STANDARD routed undecided business questions to the issue tracker — yet the pilot repository has no tracker. The adopting agent invented `docs/context/BACKLOG.md`, violating the taxonomy in §4: a context chapter represents **imperative, timeless** current state, whereas a backlog is a list of pending items. At the same time, there was no canonical place to record **`NNNN` number reservations** — the collision mitigation across parallel PRs required by §5 without specifying where to record it (the pilot reserved ADRs 0013–0018 ad hoc, with no official home).

## Decision Drivers

- The conceptual boundary of context chapters (§4) is what prevents multiple sources of truth — it must not be breached.
- Trackerless repositories are a real case; requiring an external tracker creates disproportionate adoption friction.
- Reserving `NNNN` identifiers needs a ledger versioned alongside the documents it numbers.

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Require an issue tracker

**Pros:** pending items live where pending items normally belong.

**Cons:** imposes an external dependency just to adopt the standard; the pilot already demonstrated the friction.

### Option 2 — Backlog as a context chapter

**Pros:** no new file structure.

**Cons:** breaks the imperative/timeless boundary; agents would load a to-do list as current system state.

### Option 3 — `docs/BACKLOG.md` at the root of `docs/`, outside validated layers

**Pros:** canonical home; context chapters stay pure; versioned alongside the docs; the `NNNN` reservation ledger lives in the same file.

**Cons:** one more file to know about (mitigated: the router points to it).

## Decision

Option 3. `docs/BACKLOG.md` is the official home for (a) pending decisions in a repository without an issue tracker and (b) the `NNNN` reservation ledger. Its prose content is free-form and **not validated** by `docs-check` as a documentary layer. When a tracker exists, it remains preferred for (a), while the ledger (b) still lives in `docs/BACKLOG.md`.

## Consequences

- `docs/context/` preserves its taxonomic purity; `BACKLOG.md` never lives there.
- §5 gains a concrete destination for number reservations.
- The file is optional: it only exists when there is a pending item or a reservation.

## Confirmation

```bash
test ! -e docs/context/BACKLOG.md   # exit 0: backlog is never a context chapter
```

## Notes

Lesson learned from the console-platon pilot (adoption on 2026-06-09).

ADR-0003.title: Frontmatter has a closed field vocabulary; unknown fields emit a warning
ADR-0003.body:
# Frontmatter has a closed field vocabulary; unknown fields emit a warning

## Context and Problem

During the pilot adoption, references to the removed "Goal" concept were migrated into an ad-hoc `relates` frontmatter field invented on the spot. The parser accepted the syntax, silently dropped the field from `index.json`, and reported nothing: 6 documents ended up with phantom metadata — present in the file, invisible to the graph and to the next agent. The rule "reject what you do not understand; never ignore silently" already applied to frontmatter *syntax* (§6), but not to frontmatter *keys*.

## Decision Drivers

- Validator principle: nothing passes silently.
- Legitimate extensibility exists — adopting repositories may need custom fields.
- The cost of a warning is low and visible; the cost of a phantom field is invisible and compounding.

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Unknown field is an error

**Pros:** unbreakable vocabulary.

**Cons:** kills legitimate extension; forces adopters to fork the validator for any extra field.

### Option 2 — Status quo: accept syntax and silently drop unknown keys

**Pros:** zero implementation cost.

**Cons:** reproduces the `relates` bug — dead metadata that nobody notices being born.

### Option 3 — Unknown field emits a warning

**Pros:** surfaces on the very first run; does not block merges; extension remains possible, provided it is deliberate.

**Cons:** ignored warnings accumulate noise (acceptable: warnings do not block merges).

## Decision

Option 3. The official vocabulary is `status`, `date`, `builds-on`, `superseded-by`, `implemented-by`, `deciders`. Any field outside this set emits a **warning** in `docs-check`. Extending the vocabulary in an adopting repository is permitted, provided it is deliberate: record the custom field in an ADR within that repository, or remove it.

## Consequences

- The pilot's `relates` fields surface immediately as 6 warnings on the first run after updating the script.
- Adding a new standard-wide field requires updating both `STANDARD.md` and `docs-check` — a governed vocabulary rather than organic drift.

## Confirmation

```bash
grep -q "fora do vocabulário" scripts/docs-check   # exit 0: check exists in the validator
```

## Notes

Lesson learned from the console-platon pilot (adoption on 2026-06-09).

ADR-0004.title: Bootstrapping and updating an adopting repo is an idempotent script in casa-standard
ADR-0004.body:
# Bootstrapping and updating an adopting repo is an idempotent script in casa-standard

## Context and Problem

§10 covered adoption in an existing repository as a manual ritual and did not cover new projects at all. Cloning `casa-standard` copies the *identity* of the reference repo itself (its own `AGENTS.md`, its own ADRs, its own `BACKLOG.md`), rather than a clean project skeleton. Manual copying leaves broken pointers — the router template referenced `STANDARD.md`, which does not exist in the target repository. Furthermore, there was no mechanism to **update** the toolchain (`docs-check`, templates) across repositories that had already adopted CASA: every repository stayed frozen on the snapshot from the day files were copied.

## Decision Drivers

- Automation > discipline: "how to start or update" must be a command, not a checklist.
- Every fact lives in a single file: no second template repository to keep in sync.
- Cover **all** repository states: empty, greenfield, legacy, or with pre-existing ADR/SDD docs.
- Never destroy content or make editorial decisions for the adopter: repository content belongs to the adopter, and migration judgment is human.
- Lay the groundwork for version governance (Appendix A.4) at zero cost today.

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Manual checklist in README

**Pros:** zero implementation cost.

**Cons:** discipline without validation; the pilot proved that gaps turn into improvisation.

### Option 2 — GitHub template repository ("Use this template")

**Pros:** native UX for greenfield repositories.

**Cons:** creates a second source of truth (templates and validator duplicated across two repositories, guaranteeing sync rot); covers neither existing repositories nor toolchain updates.

### Option 3 — Idempotent script inside `casa-standard` (`casa-init`)

**Pros:** single source of truth (lives right next to what it distributes); handles greenfield, legacy adoption, and updates with the exact same command; testable in the standard's own CI (so CI *proves* that every bootstrapped repo starts green).

**Cons:** one more script to maintain — mitigated by scenario tests in CI.

## Decision

Option 3. `scripts/casa-init <target>` installs and updates CASA infrastructure under three ownership rules: **toolchain belongs to the tool** (`docs-check`, `pre-commit`, templates — overwritten when different); **identity belongs to the repo** (`AGENTS.md` is created from the template only when absent and never overwritten — except for the `casa-standard-ref` line, which the tool owns and stamps); **gate follows ADR-0001** (remote → CI; no remote → hook; no `.git` → prints guidance). Content migration remains human (§10): the script diagnoses issues via `docs-check` and reports them without making editorial decisions. Detailed behavior: SPEC-0001.

## Consequences

- A new project starts green with a single command; an adopting repository updates its toolchain by re-running the same command.
- Every adopting router gains `casa-standard-ref` — the seed for Appendix A.4 (identifying outdated toolchains becomes a query instead of a manual audit).
- `casa-standard` CI tests bootstrap scenarios (`scripts/test-casa-init`).
- The distributed CI workflow becomes a dedicated template (`docs/templates/docs-check.workflow.yml`), separated from `casa-standard`'s own CI workflow.

## Confirmation

```bash
test -x scripts/casa-init && scripts/test-casa-init >/dev/null   # exit 0: bootstrap exists and scenarios pass
```

## Notes

Trigger: a real adoption question ("if I clone the repo, I bring `casa-standard`'s own `AGENTS.md` along with it"). First `NNNN` reservation recorded through the `docs/BACKLOG.md` ledger (ADR-0002).

ADR-0005.title: Bootstrap distribution is a thin curl|sh fetcher in the repository itself
ADR-0005.body:
# Bootstrap distribution is a thin curl|sh fetcher in the repository itself

## Context and Problem

ADR-0004 created `casa-init`, but the transport mechanism was still "clone `casa-standard` and run the script" — a two-step ritual leaving behind a throwaway clone. Both npm (`npm create casa`) and a self-contained shell bundle were evaluated. npm is blocked on credentials and setup (no npm login on the machine, no organization on the registry, and the `casa` package name is squatted — workaroundable via `create-casa`, but still requiring an account, CI publish tokens, and 2FA maintenance). Meanwhile, the repository is already public on GitHub: URL-based distribution infrastructure already exists at zero extra cost.

## Decision Drivers

- Every fact lives in a single file: what lands in the adopting repo must come directly from the canonical state of `casa-standard`.
- Zero new infrastructure dependencies (accounts, tokens, publish pipelines).
- `curl | sh` has a well-deserved bad reputation — the script must be auditable, ref-pinnable, and immune to truncated downloads, or it does not ship.
- The version-stamping mechanism must serve a future npm channel equally well.

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — npm (`create-casa`, via `npm create casa`)

**Pros:** registry with semantic versioning; familiar UX for JavaScript teams.

**Cons:** blocked on npm org/credentials; publish pipeline + token/2FA maintenance; published artifact lags behind the repository; `casa` name is squatted.

### Option 2 — Self-contained script (toolchain embedded as heredocs/base64)

**Pros:** single file; works offline.

**Cons:** embeds a **copy** of the toolchain — a second source of truth unless regenerated by CI on every change, recreating the exact class of problem rejected in ADR-0004. Only justified for air-gapped environments, which is not our case.

### Option 3 — Thin fetcher (`install.sh`) in the repository itself

**Pros:** embeds nothing — downloads the repository tarball at execution time (canonical `main` or a pinned ref); ~60 auditable lines; zero new infrastructure; testable offline via a local tarball.

**Cons:** requires network access at runtime (mitigated: `CASA_TARBALL` for offline/test runs); carries the `curl|sh` stigma (mitigated by the rules below).

## Decision

Option 3. Ship `install.sh` at the repository root, invoked via `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/atplus-digital/casa-standard/main/install.sh | sh`, governed by four non-negotiable rules: (1) entire script body wrapped in `main()`, invoked on the very last line — a truncated download executes nothing; (2) writes only to `mktemp` (cleaned up via `trap`) and to the target directory — no `sudo`, no `$HOME` mutation, no global installation; (3) pinnable by ref (`CASA_REF=v1.0.0`); (4) no security theater — a checksum fetched from the exact same origin as the script verifies nothing and is omitted. The downloaded SHA/ref is passed into `casa-init` via the `CASA_STANDARD_REF` environment variable and becomes the router's stamp. Detailed behavior: SPEC-0002.

## Consequences

- Bootstrapping becomes a single clone-free command; toolchain updates use the exact same command.
- `casa-init` gains `CASA_STANDARD_REF` > git precedence — if a future npm channel (`create-casa` published by CI) is ever introduced, it reuses the same mechanism (deferred, not discarded).
- `README.md` also documents the two-step path (download, inspect, execute) for security-conscious auditors.
- CI tests the installer offline (`scripts/test-install`, using local tarballs).

## Confirmation

```bash
sh -n install.sh && [ "$(tail -1 install.sh)" = 'main "$@"' ]   # syntax ok + anti-truncation guard
```

## Notes

Trigger: distribution question ("`npm install casa`?"). npm was evaluated and deferred in this decision; if revisited, it will be introduced via a new ADR superseding or extending this one.

ADR-0006.title: Gate adapter is selected by remote host — pre-commit hook is the universal fallback
ADR-0006.body:
# Gate adapter is selected by remote host — pre-commit hook is the universal fallback

## Context and Problem

ADR-0001 defined T1 gate dispatch as "has remote → CI workflow; no remote → pre-commit hook". `casa-init` implemented that check by asking only *whether* a remote exists, not *which host* it points to — while the only CI adapter shipped is for GitHub Actions (`.github/workflows/docs-check.yml`). In a repository hosted on GitLab, Bitbucket, or another git server, `casa-init` installs a workflow file that **never executes**, yet the confirmation command from ADR-0001 (`test -f .github/workflows/docs-check.yml`) still passes. Result: a decorative gate masquerading as legitimate T1 — the exact "T1 in name only" failure mode that ADR-0001 exists to prevent. Non-GitHub remotes ended up in a *worse* state than repositories with no remote at all (which at least received the pre-commit hook).

## Decision Drivers

- Standard design criterion: tool-enforced validation, not discipline — and a workflow that never runs is worse than having no gate, because it simulates protection.
- STANDARD Appendix A: extensions enter only when a real symptom appears. We have no GitLab adopter today; writing CI adapters for hypothetical hosts is premature complexity.
- On GitLab, CI lives in a single root file (`.gitlab-ci.yml`); creating or merging into it would violate `casa-init`'s contract of never mutating adopter-owned files (SPEC-0001).
- The pre-commit hook is already a legitimate T1 gate (ADR-0001) and is completely host-agnostic.

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Keep "has remote → GitHub workflow"

**Pros:** zero implementation cost.

**Cons:** decorative gate on every non-GitHub host; violates ADR-0001 itself.

### Option 2 — Per-host CI adapters (GitLab, Bitbucket, … templates)

**Pros:** native CI on every host.

**Cons:** speculative work with zero adopters; on GitLab it requires merging into a repo-owned file (breaking the additive-only contract); maintenance matrix grows with no real symptom to justify it.

### Option 3 — Host-based dispatch: GitHub → workflow; any other host → hook + WARNING

**Pros:** closes the gap across every non-GitHub host at once using the fallback that already exists; stays honest (the WARNING states that native CI for that host is not bundled and guides manual integration); preserves the additive contract.

**Cons:** hooks remain bypassable via `--no-verify` (already accepted in ADR-0001); self-hosted GitHub Enterprise on a custom domain falls back to the hook (acceptable: the WARNING explains how to wire CI).

## Decision

Option 3. `casa-init` inspects remote URLs: if a remote points to `github.com`, it installs the GitHub Actions workflow (as before); **for any other host, it installs the pre-commit hook and emits a WARNING** advising the team to wire `scripts/docs-check` into their host's CI; when there is no remote, it installs the hook as in ADR-0001. A native CI adapter for another host will only be added when a real adopter uses that host (Appendix A) — and likely as a documented snippet rather than a generated file.

## Consequences

- Non-GitHub remotes get a real gate (pre-commit hook) instead of a dead workflow file.
- The core principle of ADR-0001 stands intact: automated gate via CI **or** pre-commit hook, never discipline; only the dispatch rule changes — which is why this ADR supersedes ADR-0001.
- SPEC-0001 (EARS 7 and 12) and STANDARD §3 updated in the same commit that accepts this ADR.
- GitHub Enterprise on a custom domain falls back to the hook; teams wanting the Actions workflow can copy `docs/templates/docs-check.workflow.yml` manually — `casa-init` preserves it.

## Confirmation

```bash
# in an adopting repo: the installed gate matches the remote host
git config --get-regexp '^remote\..*\.url$' | grep -q 'github\.com' \
  && test -f .github/workflows/docs-check.yml \
  || grep -q docs-check .git/hooks/pre-commit          # exit 0: gate matches the host
```

## Notes

Symptom raised during the 2026-06-12 review ("what happens to CASA when git is hosted on GitLab?"). Scenarios covered by `scripts/test-casa-init` (EARS-7 and EARS-12 of SPEC-0001).

ADR-0007.title: Versioned governance and core invariants enter the CASA core
ADR-0007.body:
# Versioned governance and core invariants enter the CASA core

## Context and Problem

CASA already stamped `casa-standard-ref` in the router, but that field only recorded which tool snapshot a repository was bootstrapped from. It did not answer the most important question for an adopter: "which version of the normative contract does this repository promise to follow?". At the same time, the agent entry point (`AGENTS.md`) had minimal validation, Specs could reach final states while still containing template placeholders or open questions, and immutability of accepted ADRs remained deferred to Appendix A. The result was a standard with strong intent, yet missing enforcement right on the invariants that protect adopting repositories the most.

## Decision Drivers

- The standard must evolve without silently shifting the contract underneath adopters.
- The router is load-bearing: if it is incomplete, the agent starts off wrong.
- Accepted and implemented Specs must be decided and verifiable, not merely syntactically formatted.
- Accepted ADRs are the repository's causal memory; substantive inline edits erase the decision trail.
- The `casa-standard` reference repository must prove these invariants in its own CI.

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Leave everything to PR review discipline

**Pros:** zero implementation cost.

**Cons:** contradicts CASA's core design criterion; gaps surface late, after an adopting repository already trusts the standard.

### Option 2 — Introduce a new tier for governance and strict checks

**Pros:** avoids increasing T1 requirements.

**Cons:** makes foundational invariants optional; T1 would continue accepting weak routers, Specs with placeholders, and mutated ADRs.

### Option 3 — Promote invariants into the core and version the contract

**Pros:** every T1 repository gets the same baseline of trust; `casa-version` decouples the normative contract from the toolchain snapshot; migration becomes explicit.

**Cons:** existing adopters need to run `casa-init` to receive the new metadata field and resolve issues that previously slipped through.

## Decision

Option 3. CASA introduces `casa-version` in the router, maintained by `casa-init` alongside `casa-standard-ref`. Version 1.1 promotes into the core: baseline router validation, stricter validation of Specs in final states, verification that `implemented-by` entries resolve to existing paths, and an optional CI lint enforcing immutability of accepted ADRs. The standard's maintainer in `STANDARD.md` also stops being a placeholder and becomes explicit.

## Consequences

- Adopting repositories can distinguish "toolchain came from commit X" from "repository follows CASA contract 1.1".
- `docs-check` fails early when the router lacks CASA metadata or a global DoD.
- `accepted` and `implemented` Specs can no longer retain open questions or DoD placeholders.
- `implemented` Specs must point `implemented-by` to real paths in the repository.
- CI can block any body mutation in an accepted ADR by diffing against the PR base branch.

## Confirmation

```bash
python3 scripts/docs-check --check-adr-immutability --base-ref origin/main
bash scripts/test-docs-check
```

## Notes

Trigger: the 2026-06-13 standard review, which identified undefined governance, partial versioning, under-validated routers, loose Spec closure checks, and ADR immutability still sitting outside the core.

ADR-0008.title: Recognized capabilities: router declaration triggers a content invariant (closed registry)
ADR-0008.body:
# Recognized capabilities: router declaration triggers a content invariant (closed registry)

## Context and Problem

`docs-check` already implements "declaration triggers validation" in at least six places, all ad hoc: context pointer resolution (if the router cites `docs/context/X.md`, the file must exist), conditional Spec rules by `status`, closed frontmatter vocabulary (ADR-0003), tier T0/T1 rules, optional ADR immutability linting, and remote-host gate dispatch (ADR-0006). Every one follows the exact same pattern: a signal declared by the repository activates a rule **already known to the validator**.

What was missing was applying this pattern where it yields concrete value: context chapters. §2 and §4 already **name** `docs/context/TESTS.md` as a canonical chapter, yet declaring that chapter only guaranteed that the file existed — not that it fulfilled its purpose (stating the canonical test command). The danger when addressing this is sliding into an open "plugin/module system" where each adopting repository supplies its own custom validation rules — complexity sustained by discipline (nobody validates the module's validator), which CASA's core thesis explicitly rejects.

## Decision Drivers

- Validation by tool, not by discipline (core thesis of the standard; ADR-0006 criterion: "a gate that does not execute is worse than no gate").
- Determinism: CI results must never be a function of which files happen to sit on disk — only of what is **declared** in the router.
- Every fact lives in a single file: the triggered rule lives in `docs-check`, not duplicated in a per-repo manifest.
- Closed-vocabulary precedent (ADR-0003): extension is permitted, but **deliberate and centralized** — recorded in the standard, never improvised per adopter.
- Real, narrow symptom: `TESTS.md` is the first capability worth hardening; there is no symptom justifying a generic rule engine.

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Open module system (adopting repo brings its own validator)

**Pros:** maximum extensibility; every repository plugs in whatever it wants.

**Cons:** inverts authority — rules live in adopter-supplied modules that nothing validates; multiplies the maintenance matrix (N modules × validation × version × tests); destroys auditability (you can no longer read `docs-check` to know what the gate checks); re-imports as plugins the process tracking that §3 deliberately pushed out to the issue tracker.

### Option 2 — Trigger by physical file presence on disk

**Pros:** "if `TESTS.md` exists, validate it" feels intuitive.

**Cons:** action at a distance — CI status becomes a function of stray files appearing in the tree rather than declared intent. Breaks the determinism preserved everywhere else in CASA (IDs derived from paths, gates derived from remote host). Across CASA, positive triggers are always **declarations**, never mere file presence; the only disk scan (tree hygiene) hunts exclusively for trash and never assigns positive semantics to a file.

### Option 3 — CLOSED registry of recognized chapters, triggered by router declaration

**Pros:** generalizes what the validator already does (pointer resolution) without inventing a plugin engine; the trigger is the router declaration (deterministic, aligned with Principle 2); the rule lives inside `docs-check`, versioned and tested; the set is closed and grows only via ADR.

**Cons:** adding a new capability requires a PR in `casa-standard` (no adopter self-service) — acceptable and intentional: the exact same deliberate friction as the closed frontmatter vocabulary.

## Decision

Option 3. `docs-check` maintains a **closed** registry of recognized context chapters (`RECOGNIZED_CHAPTERS`). When the router **declares** one of them in its Context Map, the validator enforces a **content** invariant that it already knows. The trigger is always the router declaration, never physical file presence on disk; the rule always lives in the validator, never supplied by the adopting repository. The first — and for now sole — member is `docs/context/TESTS.md`, which must contain at least one canonical command inside a fenced code block (using the same criterion as the global DoD). New capabilities enter like any other normative change (§10): an ADR in `casa-standard` + updates to §8 and `docs-check` in the same PR. This backward-compatible change promotes the contract to `casa-version` 1.2.

## Consequences

- Declaring `TESTS.md` goes beyond "the file exists" and guarantees that the chapter fulfills its operational role — with zero plugin machinery.
- The path for `SECURITY.md`, `MIGRATIONS.md`, etc. stays open yet **narrow**: each addition is a registry entry defended by an ADR, not an unvalidated script dropped into an adopter repo.
- Explicitly **out of scope**: validating external GitHub Projects process/state (service-side truth belongs in a GitHub Action, not `docs-check`) and any adopter-supplied custom validation logic.
- `casa-init` distributes `context.TESTS.template.md`; adopting the capability means copying it to `docs/context/TESTS.md` and linking it from the router.

## Confirmation

```bash
python3 scripts/docs-check                    # exit 0: reference repo stays green
bash scripts/test-docs-check                  # exit 0: TESTS capability scenarios pass
```

## Notes

Trigger: the 2026-06-20 standard review on "further standardizing agent workflows" concluded that the real leverage is not adding a process layer, but making explicit the "declaration triggers validation" mechanism that `docs-check` already uses — with `TESTS.md` as its first member. Detailed behavior in SPEC-0004.

ADR-0009.title: CLAUDE.md bridge: hosts that do not read AGENTS.md receive an import file created by casa-init
ADR-0009.body:
# CLAUDE.md bridge: hosts that do not read AGENTS.md receive an import file created by casa-init

## Context and Problem

The CASA router lives in `AGENTS.md` (§4) — the filename with broad multi-vendor adoption (Cursor, Codex, Opencode, and similar tools). Claude Code, however, **does not read `AGENTS.md`**: its project memory file is `CLAUDE.md`, and Anthropic's official documentation explicitly recommends, for repositories standardized on `AGENTS.md`, a `CLAUDE.md` file that imports it via `@AGENTS.md`. As a result, a repository bootstrapped by `casa-init` was born with its router **invisible to the primary coding agent used across company projects** (issue #7).

The symptom had already surfaced in the field: `linee-chat` manually created a `CLAUDE.md` containing just `@AGENTS.md` — every adopter rediscovering the blind spot and patching it through human discipline, the exact failure mode the standard rejects.

## Decision Drivers

- **Every fact lives in a single file** (Principle 2): router content must never be duplicated per agent host.
- **Complexity sustained by automation**: the bridge must be installed and restored by tooling (`casa-init`), never by an onboarding checklist.
- **Portability**: the solution must work across Windows, Linux, and macOS without elevated privileges — symlinks fail this requirement on Windows.
- **Closed-registry precedent** (ADR-0008): host accommodations enter deliberately and centrally, never improvised per adopting repository.
- The ban on `@import` inside the router (§4) exists to protect context budget against inlining heavy chapters — not to prevent importing the router itself, which is always-loaded by definition.

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Rename the router to `CLAUDE.md`

**Pros:** no extra file needed for Claude Code.

**Cons:** inverts the problem — other agent hosts read `AGENTS.md`, not `CLAUDE.md`; couples the standard to a single vendor's filename, going against multi-vendor convergence on `AGENTS.md`.

### Option 2 — Symlink `CLAUDE.md → AGENTS.md`

**Pros:** single source without a second text file.

**Cons:** symlinks require elevated privileges or Developer Mode on Windows (a real adopter environment); degrade into materialized copies in zip archives and certain git clients; Claude Code's own docs note this caveat.

### Option 3 — Duplicate router content in both files

**Pros:** none that survive a single week.

**Cons:** creates multiple sources of truth; violates Principle 2 head-on; diverges on the very first edit.

### Option 4 — Bridge file `CLAUDE.md` containing `@AGENTS.md`, created by `casa-init` when absent

**Pros:** matches the host's official recommendation; portable plain-text file; `@import` expands the full router at launch — the exact desired semantics since the router is always-loaded; installed and restored by tooling; provides a sanctioned home for Claude Code-specific instructions (below the import) without polluting the multi-host router.

**Cons:** one extra file at the repository root; the list of per-host bridges requires maintenance (currently just one).

## Decision

Option 4. `casa-init` creates, **when absent**, a minimal `CLAUDE.md` from `docs/templates/CLAUDE.template.md` whose first non-comment line is `@AGENTS.md`. An existing `CLAUDE.md` is **repository identity** — it is never overwritten or mutated; if it does not contain `@AGENTS.md`, `casa-init` emits a WARNING. The set of per-host bridges is **closed** and lives in `casa-init` — today only Claude Code requires a bridge; any new host enters via an ADR in this repository (same deliberate governance cost as ADR-0008). `docs-check` does **not** validate the bridge: the normative contract stays host-agnostic, while restoring a missing bridge belongs to `casa-init` (every update recreates it if deleted). Backward-compatible change: promotes the contract to `casa-version` 1.3.

## Consequences

- Newly bootstrapped repositories are immediately readable by Claude Code with zero manual steps; existing adopters receive the bridge on their next `casa-init` run.
- The exception to "never use `@import` in the router" becomes explicit and bounded: the bridge imports the router by design, while §4's ban continues to apply to context chapters.
- `CLAUDE.md` becomes the sanctioned place for Claude Code-specific instructions — placed below `@AGENTS.md`, leaving `AGENTS.md` untouched.
- Explicitly **out of scope**: validating `CLAUDE.md` in `docs-check`, or adding bridges for hosts that already read `AGENTS.md` natively.

## Confirmation

```bash
bash scripts/test-casa-init     # exit 0: bridge scenarios (SPEC-0005) pass
python3 scripts/docs-check      # exit 0: reference repo stays green
```

## Notes

Trigger: issue #7 and verification against Claude Code's official documentation (*How Claude remembers your project*) confirming that `AGENTS.md` is not read natively — and recommending the `@AGENTS.md` shim. Detailed behavior in SPEC-0005. This repository practices the decision: the root `CLAUDE.md` is an instantiated bridge.

ADR-0010.title: casa-version is the repo's promise: casa-init does not stamp it; docs-check flags drift
ADR-0010.body:
# casa-version is the repo's promise: casa-init does not stamp it; docs-check flags drift

## Context and Problem

§10 defines `casa-version` as "the normative contract that the adopting repository **promises** to follow" (ADR-0007). Yet `casa-init` trampled that promise: `upsert_router_meta` unconditionally overwrote `casa-version` on every run — even downgrading it if invoked from an older snapshot. In practice, the field had become an **echo of the toolchain**, redundant with `casa-standard-ref`.

Issue #15 proposed a drift warning comparing the router's declared version against the installed toolchain version. Adversarial review of that proposal (three independent reviewers, 2026-07-05) refuted the original design via sandbox reproduction: as long as `casa-init` auto-stamped `casa-version`, declaration and toolchain traveled together along the sanctioned path — **the warning would never fire**. Worse, the motivating field case was completely unreachable: `console-platon` (CASA 1.1) had gained a GitHub remote after initial adoption and had no active gate at all — no warning embedded inside an updated toolchain can reach a repository that never updates.

## Decision Drivers

- **A promise belongs to the promisor.** A field overwritten by a tool promises nothing; §10 always said "promises to follow".
- **Warnings must be reachable and actionable** — "a gate that simulates protection is worse than no gate" (ADR-0006 criterion).
- **No network in the gate** (ADR-0005/ADR-0006): version comparison must remain local and deterministic.
- Upgrading the contract requires reading `CHANGELOG.md` and verifying compliance — a deliberate human/agent decision in the adopting repo, never a side effect of copying scripts.

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Keep auto-stamping and warn by comparing declaration vs. toolchain

**Pros:** requires no change to `casa-init`.

**Cons:** empirically refuted — `casa-init` equalizes both sides in the same run (sandbox: router bumped 1.1 → 1.3 automatically); the check compares an echo against its own source and never fires in the sanctioned workflow. Window-dressing check: looks like protection, never executes.

### Option 2 — Check version against upstream over the network

**Pros:** would detect absolute lag (repositories that never run `casa-init`).

**Cons:** makes the gate non-deterministic and network-dependent in CI and pre-commit — violating ADR-0005/ADR-0006. Rejected; absolute lag is recorded in Appendix A.5 instead.

### Option 3 — `casa-version` becomes repo identity; `docs-check` flags incoherence

**Pros:** the promise becomes a genuine promise again; the warning gains real leverage (after updating the toolchain, the older declaration stays put — catching up on the contract becomes a deliberate act after reading `CHANGELOG.md`); local, deterministic, zero network.

**Cons:** the contract version now lives in two constants (`casa-init` and `docs-check`) — duplication guarded by a consistency test in `casa-standard` CI.

## Decision

Option 3, in two parts:

1. **`casa-init`**: in an existing router, updates only `casa-standard-ref` (owned by the tool); `casa-version` is **inserted only when absent** (bootstrapping a required metadata key with the current contract version) and **never modified afterward** — it is repository identity, just like the rest of the router (SPEC-0001, edge case 13).
2. **`docs-check`**: gains the `CONTRACT_VERSION` constant (the contract version implemented by this toolchain) and compares it against the router's declaration by `(major, minor)`: declaration **lower** → contract-behind warning ("read `CHANGELOG.md` and update `casa-version` once the repo satisfies the new contract"); declaration **higher** → toolchain-behind warning ("run `casa-init` from a current snapshot"). **Warning, never error** — backward-compatible updates must never break an adopter's gate (§10). A malformed `casa-version` remains a format error as before, without stacking the drift warning on top.

Symptom that promotes the warning to an error (Appendix A discipline applied to severity): if an adopter operates **≥2 minor versions behind for more than one release** and suffers a costly migration or contract incident as a result — at that point, contract-behind promotes to an error via a new ADR.

## Consequences

- Running `casa-init` ≥1.4 for the first time on an older repository updates the toolchain and **leaves `casa-version` untouched** — the warning surfaces on the next gate run, and contract catch-up is decided by someone who read `CHANGELOG.md`. Auto-stamping no longer masks unverified contract upgrades.
- Silent promise downgrades (running `casa-init` from an older checkout) become impossible.
- **Beyond the reach** of any local check: a repository that never runs `casa-init` and has no active gate (the actual state of `console-platon` at the time). Recorded as Appendix A.5 — adopter update cadence is process, not gate.
- Every contract version bump now touches two constants; the consistency test in `test-casa-init` turns forgetfulness into red CI inside `casa-standard`.

## Confirmation

```bash
bash scripts/test-casa-init     # exit 0: promise preserved + constants synchronized
bash scripts/test-docs-check    # exit 0: warning scenarios (SPEC-0006) pass
python3 scripts/docs-check      # exit 0: reference repo stays green
```

## Notes

Trigger: issue #15 + adversarial review on 2026-07-05 (three independent reviewers; the skeptic reproduced the auto-stamp echo in a sandbox). Detailed behavior: SPEC-0006 (warnings) and SPEC-0001 (`casa-init` ownership rule, evolved in the same PR).

ADR-0011.title: docs-check flags backlog inside docs/context/ — location warning
ADR-0011.body:
# docs-check flags backlog inside docs/context/ — location warning

## Context and Problem

ADR-0002 and §5.1 place the backlog at `docs/BACKLOG.md`, **outside** `docs/context/` — "a backlog is pending work, not imperative state". ADR-0002's own `## Confirmation` was already executable: `test ! -e docs/context/BACKLOG.md`. Yet no tool actually ran that check: the rule lived solely in prose.

Field result (2026-07-05): **console-platon** — the pilot repository itself — still kept its backlog at `docs/context/BACKLOG.md` (even declared as a chapter in the router), `docs-check` passed green, and the drift had aged silently since initial migration without anything flagging it. A rule sustained by discipline rotted, just as the thesis predicts.

## Decision Drivers

- Mechanize what the standard already decided (ADR-0002) — this is not a new rule, it turns an accepted decision's Confirmation into validator code.
- Backward compatibility (§10): introducing the check must not break the gate of repositories currently in drift.
- Cross-filesystem determinism: developers run on NTFS/APFS (case-insensitive) while CI runs on ext4 (case-sensitive) — the check must behave identically on both.

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Leave the rule in prose

**Pros:** zero implementation cost.

**Cons:** already failed — the pilot drifted for weeks and nobody noticed. Pure discipline.

### Option 2 — Immediate error

**Pros:** forces immediate convergence.

**Cons:** the very first toolchain update would break `console-platon`'s gate — a backward-compatible minor release cannot do that (§10).

### Option 3 — Centralized warning, case-insensitive via directory listing

**Pros:** immediate visibility without breaking existing gates; deterministic (lists `docs/context/` entries and compares `entry.lower() == "backlog.md"`, yielding the exact same result on NTFS and ext4); rule lives in the validator (ADR-0008).

**Cons:** warnings can be ignored — mitigated by naming the exact symptom that promotes it to an error.

## Decision

Option 3. `docs-check` lists `docs/context/` and emits a **warning** for any file whose lowercase name is `backlog.md`, instructing the user to move it to `docs/BACKLOG.md` and update router pointers.

Symptom that promotes the warning to an error: a repository **creating** a brand-new `docs/context/BACKLOG.md` while already on toolchain ≥1.4 (an active warning ignored at creation time needs to block), or a known adopter's drift surviving two releases with the warning active — in either case, promotion to error happens via a new ADR.

## Consequences

- `console-platon` sees the drift on its very next toolchain update — without breaking deployments.
- `docs-reserve` (issue #12) gains a verifiable prerequisite: it can refuse to operate while the backlog sits in `docs/context/` rather than silently creating a second backlog.
- `docs/BACKLOG.md` at the root of `docs/` remains the canonical home and triggers no warning.

## Confirmation

```bash
bash scripts/test-docs-check    # exit 0: location scenarios (SPEC-0006) pass
python3 scripts/docs-check      # exit 0: reference repo stays green
```

## Notes

Trigger: issue #17, backed by evidence from the 2026-07-05 adopter fleet audit. Detailed behavior in SPEC-0006.

ADR-0012.title: Spec DoD exercises edge cases; incremental delivery splits the spec or cuts scope
ADR-0012.body:
# Spec DoD exercises edge cases; incremental delivery splits the spec or cuts scope

## Context and Problem

The executable DoD (§7) is the sole link between a Spec and actual runtime code behavior — `docs-check` validates documentation structure, never application runtime. When a Spec's DoD is purely generic, the gate stays green while the contract lies. Two field symptoms surfaced in the 2026-07-05 audit:

1. **`implemented` Spec whose code ignores what the Spec defines.** `qualimonitor` #45/#46: `incident_config` (quorum, hysteresis, cooldown) and `interval_seconds` were specified in the Spec, collected in the UI, persisted in the database — and completely ignored by the runtime worker. Its SPEC-0009 enumerated 13 EARS edge cases yet had a DoD that was a strict subset of the repository's global DoD (`typecheck`/`lint`/`test`/`build`): nothing in it exercised quorum. Green gate, false contract.
2. **`accepted`/`implemented` Spec with deliberately partial delivery.** `linee-chat` SPEC-0002: "full schema migration — currently partial". A half-delivered umbrella spec has no honest status in the vocabulary — "what counts as done" becomes subjective interpretation. By contrast, SPEC-0018 in the same repository practiced clean scope cutting: "Out of scope (decided)" pointing backfill work to the backlog.

## Decision Drivers

- Acceptance criteria are commands, not paragraphs (Principle 4) — but a **generic** repo command closes the repo's loop, not the spec's loop.
- Atomic closure (§5.2/§9) and keeping delivery grouping out of CASA docs (§3): phasing increments is the job of PRs and the issue tracker, not of perpetually half-implemented specs.
- Honesty in the standard: non-mechanizable rules enter explicitly marked as human review (just as §5.2 already treats gotcha propagation), never pretending to be an automated gate.
- The reference repository must never contradict itself: a heuristic check that triggers permanent false warnings in `casa-standard` itself trains agents to ignore warnings.

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Normative prose only, without an ADR

**Pros:** minimal PR.

**Cons:** would be the first contract bump without a causal record (1.1 → 1.4 all have ADRs); ADR-0008 already established that "normative changes enter like any §10 change: via ADR".

### Option 2 — Prose + mechanical "Spec DoD ⊆ global DoD" warning in `docs-check`

**Pros:** mechanizes the signal; across field measurements (80 specs across 5 repos), the subset check caught 15 cases including the motivating bug, with only 2–3 tolerable false positives.

**Cons:** refuted by dogfooding — in `casa-standard` itself, the global DoD is the **union** of per-spec test suites (`test-casa-init` exercises SPEC-0001 and is listed in the global DoD): all 6 specs here are **legitimate** subsets and would emit permanent false warnings in the reference repo. Exempting by allowlist or `implemented-by` would be ad-hoc heuristics — clever complexity, not trustworthy automation.

### Option 3 — Normative prose marked as human review + heuristic recorded as a future extension

**Pros:** brings the rule into the contract with an honest verification mechanism (human PR review, matching §5.2 closure rules); documents the exact false-positive obstacle for anyone revisiting automated detection (issue #16).

**Cons:** relies on human review until someone designs a check that does not misfire on the reference repo.

## Decision

Option 3, in two rules:

1. **§7 — Spec DoD exercises the spec.** Every enumerated edge case must have a DoD command line — or a test invoked by that line — that exercises it; a Spec DoD whose commands are exclusively generic repo-wide checks (a subset of the router's global DoD) is a **signal of a spec lacking its own closure**. Suggested traceability: cite edge-case numbers in line comments (`npm test -- --run dns   # cases 1–4`). Verifying the case↔command link **is not mechanizable** and rests with human PR review.
2. **§5.2 — Incremental delivery splits or cuts.** Incremental delivery either **splits the spec** (each deliverable increment becomes its own spec with independent atomic closure) **or cuts the deferred increment out of the contract** (`## Fora do escopo` / `## Out of Scope` decided + item logged in backlog/tracker). Half-implemented umbrella specs do not exist. When splitting an already-accepted spec, the original transitions to `deprecated` (specs do not use `superseded-by`; §6/§8) and the new split specs reference it via `builds-on`.

Applicability: new specs and touched specs (following §10's migration rule: touched doc, migrated doc). Existing untouched stock is not retroactively non-compliant.

## Consequences

- The `qualimonitor` #45 failure mode would have been caught during spec PR review: 13 EARS cases with zero targeted test commands is now a named non-conformity.
- `linee-chat` SPEC-0002 has a clear resolution path: split (schema migration becomes its own spec) or cut (move remaining scope out of the contract and close what shipped).
- Automated subset warning stays **documented and blocked** (issue #16): implementing it requires solving the reference-repo union false positive without ad-hoc exemptions.

## Confirmation

```bash
python3 scripts/docs-check    # exit 0 — repo stays green; no new automated check
grep -q "subconjunto do DoD global" STANDARD.md   # rule is in the contract (§7)
grep -q "divide a spec" STANDARD.md               # incremental split rule too (§5.2)
```

## Notes

Trigger: issue #16, backed by field evidence from `qualimonitor` #45/#46 and `linee-chat` (SPEC-0002/0018), plus empirical measurements from the 2026-07-05 adversarial review ("identical to global DoD": 0/80 specs — inert signal; "subset of global DoD": 15/80 specs including the motivating case). Rejection of the automated gate heuristic is documented under Option 2.

ADR-0013.title: docs-reserve automates NNNN reservation; the ledger adopts a per-section table format
ADR-0013.body:
# docs-reserve automates NNNN reservation; the ledger adopts a per-section table format

## Context and Problem

CASA requires reserving the next `NNNN` identifier in `docs/BACKLOG.md` before creating an ADR or Spec (§5, ADR-0002). Performed manually, this involves picking the next number, copying the template file, setting today's date and H1 title, and logging the reservation. In parallel workflows this collides — `linee-chat` operates with multiple simultaneous worktrees reserving numbers by hand — and `docs-check` only catches duplicate IDs post-merge, when renumbering already cascades across `builds-on` references (issue #12).

Field survey (2026-07-05): adopters had already diverged into three incompatible ledger formats — prose with number ranges (`console-platon`), Markdown tables `| ID | File | Status |` (`linee-*`, `qualimonitor`), and numbered prose bullets in this repo. Any automation had to standardize a single format — and decide how to handle unparseable lines.

## Decision Drivers

- Remove error-prone manual mechanics (next number, kebab-case slug, date, template copy) without promising distributed locks that a local filesystem cannot deliver (already ruled out in issue #12).
- **Nothing passes silently** (ADR-0003): silently skipping an unreadable reservation line reintroduces the very ID collision the tool exists to prevent, now compounded by false confidence — worse than manual numbering.
- Adopt what field repos already converged on: 3 out of 5 repositories already used Markdown tables — inventing a brand-new prose syntax would create a fourth format.
- `docs-check` remains the sole gate authority (ADR-0002 stands intact: `BACKLOG.md` is not a gate-validated layer); the table format contract belongs to the **`docs-reserve` command**, not to `docs-check`.

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Keep manual reservation (status quo)

**Pros:** zero code.

**Cons:** recurring real-world pain; human typos in numbers, slugs, dates, and placeholders are exactly what cheap automation eliminates.

### Option 2 — New structured-prose format with tolerant parsing

**Pros:** resembles `casa-standard`'s previous prose ledger.

**Cons:** prose is ambiguous to parse; tolerant parsing means silently skipping unrecognized lines, causing silent collisions (violating ADR-0003); ignores field convergence on Markdown tables.

### Option 3 — Per-section Markdown table (field format) with strict, noisy parsing

**Pros:** `## Reservas ADR` / `## Reservas Spec` with `| NNNN | título | data | situação |` matches what adopters already use in practice (the parser also accepts `ADR-NNNN`/`SPEC-NNNN` in the first cell to minimize migration friction); any unparseable line inside a reservation section is **flagged** with actionable instructions, never silently ignored; `next = max(files, reservations) + 1` respects manual reservations and never reuses gaps (since renumbering cascades, §5).

**Cons:** existing prose ledgers must migrate their reservation sections to tables — cheap, and the warning tells the user exactly what to migrate.

## Decision

Option 3. Ship `scripts/docs-reserve` (zero-dependency Python 3 script, distributed in `casa-init`'s toolchain): `docs-reserve adr|spec "title" [--dry-run] [--no-emit-index]` — computes the next `NNNN`, instantiates the document from the **repo's installed template** (today's date; H1 = title; initial status kept at the template default: `proposed`/`draft`), appends the row to the reservation table in `docs/BACKLOG.md`, and regenerates indices. Never overwrites existing files; rejects titles that yield an empty ASCII slug; **refuses to run** if a misplaced backlog exists under `docs/context/` (ADR-0011) rather than creating a second ledger. No manual `--id` flag (human number picking is what causes collisions; legacy doc migration uses `git mv`, not reservation) and no cancel subcommand (the table stays plain Markdown editable by hand; the rest of `BACKLOG.md` remains free-form per ADR-0002).

**Honest scope:** parallel worktrees or branches of the same repository **can still pick the same number** — each checkout only sees its own `BACKLOG.md`. What changes: a collision becomes an **early textual merge/rebase conflict on the table** rather than a post-merge duplicate ID error, and formatting/numbering typos disappear. Contemplated future extension: scanning local sibling branches (`git for-each-ref`) before suggesting a number.

## Consequences

- `CONTRIBUTING.md` and §5 now recommend `scripts/docs-reserve`; manual "Next available" lines in ledgers disappear (the command computes the next number; hand-maintained counters contradict themselves on first use).
- This repository's own `docs/BACKLOG.md` ledger migrates to the table format **in the same PR** (dogfooding).
- Repositories with prose reservation sections receive line-by-line WARNINGs until migrated — execution still proceeds, warning the user to migrate before trusting the suggested number.
- `casa-init` distributes and updates `scripts/docs-reserve` alongside the rest of the toolchain.

## Confirmation

```bash
bash scripts/test-docs-reserve   # exit 0: SPEC-0007 scenarios pass
python3 scripts/docs-check       # exit 0: reference repo stays green
```

## Notes

Trigger: issue #12; table format and loud unparsed-line warnings stem from the 2026-07-05 adversarial review (surveying the three field ledger styles and the silent-skip collision hazard). Detailed behavior: SPEC-0007.

ADR-0014.title: Where UI lives: system ADR, states in the spec, non-normative design-ref
ADR-0014.body:
# Where UI lives: system ADR, states in the spec, non-normative design-ref

## Context and Problem

None of CASA's four pillars stated where a feature's UI is specified (issue #13). That gap proved real and expensive across adopters: in `console-platon`, data/RPC specs were precise while UI specs declared "visual design out of scope" — resulting in documented pain like `platon#12` ("the single biggest reported pain point": product/plan/offer ambiguity), `platon#3` (public page lacking layout standards), and pricing logic duplicated across two components. In `linee-chat`, SPEC-0004/0010 referenced mockups with no resolvable artifact — while field repos were already versioning **local** design artifacts (`docs/mockups/*.html`, handoff directories with `tokens.css`), not just Figma URLs.

The temptation is inventing a fifth pillar or a parallel "UI spec" template. Both multiply artifacts unnecessarily; CASA already has the right places.

## Decision Drivers

- No fifth pillar and no parallel template: real features blend API and UI — maintaining two spec templates forces an extra choice on every document and invites template drift (documents without a distinct trigger are noise, §3).
- Normativity follows verifiability (Principle 4): "does it match the design?" enters the normative contract only insofar as it reduces to `exit 0/1`.
- **The reference standard must never induce fictitious DoDs**: no adopter currently runs visual-regression or automated a11y toolchains — a copy-pasteable example command that the repo does not actually have would pass `docs-check` while violating §7 undetectably (ADR-0012).
- Vocabulary extension is deliberate and centralized (ADR-0003: "a new standard-wide field requires updating both `STANDARD.md` and `docs-check`"); forcing N repositories to each write a local ADR for the same field repeats the anti-pattern documented in ADR-0009.

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Fifth pillar / "Design" documentary layer

**Pros:** obvious dedicated address.

**Cons:** creates an entire layer for a single content facet; coding agents do not consume Figma directly; duplicates what ADR + Spec already carry. Already ruled out in issue #13 itself.

### Option 2 — Separate `spec-ui.template.md` template (original issue proposal)

**Pros:** dedicated UI guidance.

**Cons:** mixed API+UI features would have to pick one template; ships a second template file into every adopter's toolchain; invites drift between templates; UI guidance is a short comment block, not a distinct document structure.

### Option 3 — ADR (design system) + Spec (UI states) + central `design-ref` + guidance block in the single template

**Pros:** reuses the two existing layers in their natural roles (dated structural decision vs. verifiable feature behavior); keeps a single spec template; adds a central frontmatter key with zero warning noise; stays consistent with ADR-0003/0008/0012.

**Cons:** less prescriptive than a dedicated UI template — mitigated by the normative note in §5.2 and template comments.

## Decision

Option 3, in four parts:

1. **Structural UI decisions → one repository ADR.** Design system choice, token strategy, responsiveness breakpoints, and mandatory view states (loading/empty/error) are dated architectural decisions inherited by feature specs via `builds-on` — never redefined per feature.
2. **Feature visual behavior → standard EARS edge cases in the Spec.** "WHEN the list is empty, the system SHALL render an empty-state with CTA" is an edge case like any other — and falls under ADR-0012: it requires a DoD line that exercises it.
3. **Visual appearance → code + executable DoD using real repository commands.** Design tokens live in code; visual regression and a11y checks enter the DoD **when the repository actually has that toolchain** — `spec.template.md` mentions those verification classes as options without providing fake copy-pasteable commands.
4. **`design-ref` enters the central closed vocabulary** (§6 + `KNOWN_KEYS`): scalar string accepting either a URL **or a relative path** (matching local-mockup practice in the field), explicitly **non-normative** — if design and code+snapshots diverge, code wins, and aesthetic fidelity belongs to `## Revisão humana` (`## Human Review`), never to an automated gate. No format validation (matching `deciders` precedent). Exported to `docs/index.json` so it is a first-class graph field rather than phantom metadata (§6). Because `KNOWN_KEYS` is global across layers, `design-ref` is also silently valid in ADRs — accepted intentionally (a design-system ADR may link its reference artifact), though Specs remain its primary home.

## Consequences

- Adopters get a normative home for UI concerns with zero new document types: §5.2 points to this ADR, and the comment block in `spec.template.md` guides UI states and honest DoDs.
- Design links gain a canonical, indexable frontmatter field — and a dead Figma link never breaks a gate (it is non-normative, and specs remain editable in any status).
- Explicitly **out of scope**: URL/path format validation on `design-ref`; mandatory visual regression testing (used only when a repo's toolchain supports it); a separate UI spec template.
- Field debt note: the **local** vocabulary extension path in §6 ("record the custom field in an ADR of the repo") does not silence the `docs-check` warning — `docs-check` does not parse adopter ADRs for custom keys, so local extensions live alongside permanent warnings. Central registration remains the noise-free path.

## Confirmation

```bash
bash scripts/test-docs-check     # design-ref scenarios (vocabulary + index) pass
python3 scripts/docs-check       # exit 0: reference repo stays green
grep -q "design-ref" STANDARD.md # semantics documented in §6
```

## Notes

Trigger: issue #13, with two refinements over the original proposal (single template; central frontmatter key) validated by adversarial review on 2026-07-05. The no-fictitious-DoD-commands rule comes from the same review: no adopter ran Storybook/axe/Percy at the time, so copyable example commands would have encouraged false DoDs. This ADR was reserved and scaffolded using `scripts/docs-reserve` (SPEC-0007) — its first production use.

ADR-0016.title: Scheduled detection of outdated contracts — network outside the gate, notification in the tracker
ADR-0016.body:
# Scheduled detection of outdated contracts — network outside the gate, notification in the tracker

## Context and Problem

ADR-0010 closed the **internal** coherence loop (router declaration vs. installed toolchain) and rejected network calls inside `docs-check` (Option 2 there): the gate must stay deterministic, runs as a local pre-commit hook on repos without GitHub, and promises offline operation. That left a named gap in Appendix A.5: **absolute lag** — an internally coherent but outdated repository (toolchain 1.1 + declaration 1.1) stays completely silent until someone remembers to run `casa-init`. Remembering is human discipline. The fleet audit on 2026-07-05 proved the symptom: every adopting repository sat 4 to 6 minor versions behind, and the only detection mechanism was a manual audit (`qualimonitor#18`).

## Decision Drivers

- Network access is acceptable **where network is natural and failure blocks nobody**: a scheduled CI job on the git host — never in a commit or PR gate.
- Notifications nobody reads become wallpaper: the alert belongs in the **issue tracker** (an actionable, deduplicated item that closes itself once resolved), right where §3 places operational tracking.
- Per-host adapter model (ADR-0006): ship the mechanism for hosts with a supported adapter (today: GitHub); other hosts remain covered by Appendix A.5 process.
- Compare by **contract version**, never by toolchain commit SHA: the SHA changes on every `casa-standard` commit and would create perpetual noise, whereas the contract version is the meaningful signal (ADR-0007).

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Network check inside `docs-check`

Rejected in ADR-0010 and remains rejected: breaks gate determinism, introduces pre-commit flakiness, and violates the offline guarantee.

### Option 2 — Offline snapshot-age warning ("toolchain is >N months old")

**Pros:** purely local.

**Cons:** non-deterministic (a function of wall-clock time: the exact same commit changes pass/warn status as time passes) and semantically wrong — old ≠ outdated (the contract may not have changed).

### Option 3 — Scheduled host workflow + testable shell script + tracker issue as notification

**Pros:** keeps network strictly outside the gate, inside a job whose failure blocks nothing (`exit 0` on external errors); surfaces lag as a GitHub issue labeled `casa-update` — opened when behind, **edited in place** (never duplicated) while still behind, and **closed automatically** once the repo catches up; encapsulates logic in a POSIX `sh` script in the toolchain (testable offline with `curl`/`gh` stubs) wrapped by a thin workflow; distributed by `casa-init` exclusively to GitHub remotes, created when absent and never overwritten (matching the gate workflow's ownership contract).

**Cons:** covers only hosts with an adapter and requires `casa-init` to have installed the workflow at least once — a repository that has never run `casa-init` since adoption remains in A.5, which is irreducibly true by definition.

## Decision

Option 3. Add to the toolchain: `scripts/casa-update-check` (POSIX `sh`; reads `casa-version` from `AGENTS.md`, fetches the latest released version from raw `CHANGELOG.md` in `casa-standard` — overridable via `CASA_SOURCE_URL` for testing or forks — and reconciles the tracker issue) plus `docs/templates/casa-update-check.workflow.yml` (weekly cron + `workflow_dispatch`, `permissions: issues: write`). Hard rules for the script: **always `exit 0`** whenever the external world fails (network outage, unparseable remote response) — enforcing router integrity belongs to `docs-check`, not here; a declared version ahead of upstream is treated as up-to-date (not this script's job to judge); at most one open issue per repository, keyed by the `casa-update` label.

## Consequences

- The update loop closes end-to-end, with each component in its proper place: **scheduled workflow** detects absolute lag (network, outside the gate) → **tracker issue** prompts running `casa-init` → `casa-init` updates the toolchain without touching `casa-version` (ADR-0010) → **`docs-check` warning** (local, deterministic) prompts deliberate verification and updating of the contract declaration.
- Appendix A.5 is updated: "external out-of-gate check" is now solved for GitHub repositories, while `casa-init` cadence on hosts without an adapter remains a team process.
- `casa-standard` does **not** install this workflow on itself (comparing the source of truth against itself is a no-op — and `casa-init` has refused self-targeting since SPEC-0001).
- Accepted cost: a second workflow file in GitHub adopters' `.github/workflows/`; GitHub automatically disables scheduled workflows on public repos after 60 days of repo inactivity — `workflow_dispatch` covers manual re-triggering.

## Confirmation

```bash
bash scripts/test-update-check   # exit 0: SPEC-0008 scenarios with stubs pass
bash scripts/test-casa-init      # exit 0: per-host workflow installation covered
python3 scripts/docs-check       # exit 0: reference repo stays green
```

## Notes

Trigger: issue #25, following up on "shouldn't `docs-check` query GitHub?" — the answer inside the gate is no (ADR-0010), and this ADR is the "yes, in the right place". Detailed behavior: SPEC-0008. Reserved and scaffolded via `docs-reserve`; an `NNNN` collision with ADR-0015 on parallel branch PR #24 occurred when creating this document and was resolved manually — live confirmation of the parallel-branch scope boundary documented in ADR-0013.

ADR-0017.title: Delivery cycle as Agent Skills: the agent executes §9; agent-driven verification is assistive, never a gate
ADR-0017.body:
# Delivery cycle as Agent Skills: the agent executes §9; agent-driven verification is assistive, never a gate

## Context and Problem

The delivery cycle (STANDARD §9) lived solely in prose: an agent had to read the standard, remember the sequence of steps, and apply every rule on its own. The very steps that STANDARD itself identifies as the most fragile links in the loop — closure propagation (gotchas → router, current state → context chapter, §5.2) and the edge-case ↔ DoD link (§7, ADR-0012) — relied entirely on human PR review, i.e., discipline.

Field evidence pointed to the exact same gap. The consolidated CASA × atplus audit report (2026-11-18) showed Specs closed with green DoDs whose tests never reached the real consequence: mocked databases standing in for database triggers (ATPlus Vision, SPEC-0049), mocked transport standing in for runtime integration (Console Platon). The review question that catches these failures — "under what broken implementation would this test still pass?" — appeared nowhere in the agent's operational workflow.

By 2026-11-18, the broader ecosystem had turned such workflows into executable agent procedures: OpenSpec ships `explore → propose → apply → verify → archive` as agent commands; Spec Kit ships `specify → plan → tasks → implement` with `analyze`. The portable open format is **Agent Skills** (agentskills.io): a `<name>/SKILL.md` directory with `name` and `description` in YAML frontmatter, where agents load only compact descriptions at session start and pull the full body on demand when a task matches. At that date, the cross-client project convention was `.agents/skills/`, while Claude Code read exclusively `.claude/skills/`.

## Decision Drivers

- **Automation over discipline:** the fragile human-only links need to become an executable procedure that the agent runs step by step.
- **The gate stays deterministic:** zero LLMs and zero network calls in the gate (ADR-0010); agent-performed verification never approves or blocks merges on its own.
- **Every fact lives in a single file:** skills point to `STANDARD.md` and toolchain scripts rather than copying normative rules.
- **Cross-agent portability:** open Agent Skills specification, with zero vendor-specific frontmatter keys.
- **Context budget discipline:** every installed skill costs its `description` (~100 tokens) in every session; keep the set small and descriptions tight.
- **Zero new obligations on adopters:** the normative contract (what the repository promises to pass) does not change.

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Keep §9 as prose only

**Pros:** zero maintenance cost.

**Cons:** the fragile closure link stays purely human; every agent session reinterprets the cycle from scratch; failures like the Vision mock gap repeat.

### Option 2 — Adopt OpenSpec wholesale

**Pros:** ready-made, actively maintained, popular workflow.

**Cons:** replaces CASA's Spec layer model (living specs + delta folders), introduces `tasks.md` (which §3 delegates to the issue tracker), and would require a breaking CASA 2.0 redesign. Worth evaluating in a dedicated pilot, not adopting by inertia.

### Option 3 — `casa-*` Agent Skills executing §9, distributed via `casa-init`

**Pros:** uses the open Agent Skills format; maps 1:1 onto CASA's existing delivery cycle; embeds the adversarial test-audit question directly into the agent's workflow; ships through the existing toolchain channel.

**Cons:** adds five skill descriptions to every session's context; requires two directory copies per adopting repo (one per host directory convention).

### Option 4 — Agent-driven verification as a blocking CI gate

**Pros:** would enforce the fragile semantic link "by force".

**Cons:** non-deterministic, incurs token cost and network calls inside the gate (violating ADR-0010); false positives block merges without a binary reproducible criterion.

## Decision

Option 3. `casa-standard` maintains five skills under `docs/templates/skills/`, one per stage of §9, using strictly portable frontmatter fields (`name`, `description`):

| Skill | Stage | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `casa-explore` | §9.4 | router → Context Map chapters → ADR/Spec subgraph → code; identifies §3 triggers |
| `casa-propose` | §9.1–3 | decides ADR / Spec / nothing, reserves IDs via `docs-reserve`, writes EARS & DoD with real repo commands |
| `casa-apply` | §9.4–5 | implements an accepted Spec until DoD is green; open questions block |
| `casa-verify` | §7, §5.2 | runs DoD + `docs-check` and audits edge-case ↔ test coverage — **assistive, never a gate** |
| `casa-close` | §9.6 | executes atomic closure in a single commit |

`casa-init` installs all five into a **closed** set of target directories: `.agents/skills/` (cross-client convention) and `.claude/skills/` (because Claude Code does not read `.agents/skills/` — exact same rationale as the `CLAUDE.md` bridge in ADR-0009). Supporting a new host directory requires an ADR. All `casa-*` skills are **toolchain-owned**: overwritten whenever they diverge from templates, whereas repo-owned skills under any other name are never touched — teams wanting custom workflows create skills under their own prefix.

Each skill links to `STANDARD.md` §N anchored at the **installed toolchain snapshot**: templates use `blob/main/` and `casa-init` rewrites links to the adopter's `casa-standard-ref` — `STANDARD.md` itself is never copied into adopting repositories. Retired or renamed CASA skills enter a retirement list that `casa-init` cleans up in adopters (only if the file carries the CASA marker, preserving unrelated third-party skills of the same name; downgrading a repo to T0 also removes previously installed `casa-*` skills). Unwritable skill paths (e.g., `.claude` is a regular file) or `.gitignore`d skill directories emit a WARNING without aborting the rest of `casa-init`.

`docs-check` does not validate skills (they are not a gate). Skills are documented in STANDARD §2 and §9 as a **backward-compatible** contract evolution, bumping the minor version to CASA 1.10 (ADR-0010) so `casa-update-check` notifies adopters.

## Consequences

- The delivery cycle becomes an executable, portable agent procedure; `/casa-verify` injects into the agent workflow the exact adversarial test question that human review kept missing.
- Every agent session pays the context budget of five short descriptions (~1,500 characters total — ten entries in clients that scan both directories), so descriptions must stay concise and specific.
- T1 adopters carry identical generated `.agents/skills/casa-*` and `.claude/skills/casa-*` trees; clients scanning both directories see duplicate names with identical instructions.
- `casa-standard` itself (`casa-standard-ref: self`, where `casa-init` refuses to run) keeps only the canonical source in `docs/templates/skills/`, without duplicating copies into `.agents/` or `.claude/`.
- Skill prose could drift relative to `STANDARD.md`: `test-casa-init` verifies frontmatter format, byte-for-byte identity across both target directories, existence of every referenced `scripts/…` tool, and existence of every cited `§N` / `§N.M` section in `STANDARD.md`. Ensuring skills do not invent standalone normative rules remains human PR review.
- Deferred to separate decisions: `docs-check --json` (structured output for `casa-verify`) and piloting OpenSpec's delta-based living-spec model.

## Confirmation

```bash
scripts/test-casa-init   # SPEC-0010: skills in both directories, identical, valid format, existing commands and sections
```

## Notes

Triggers: 2026-11-18 ecosystem review (OpenSpec, Spec Kit, Agent Skills) and the consolidated CASA × atplus field audit. Format specification: agentskills.io/specification.

ADR-0018.title: Public GitHub Pages site compiled from canonical sources with no second source of truth
ADR-0018.body:
# Public GitHub Pages site compiled from canonical sources with no second source of truth

## Context and Problem

Anyone evaluating or consulting the CASA Standard previously had to browse raw Markdown files scattered across the repository (`README.md`, `STANDARD.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/adr/`, `docs/specs/`, and `docs/templates/skills/`). There was no single public entry point readable as a polished technical specification with instant search, copyable quickstart commands, and visual navigation across the causal graph of ADRs and Specs.

At the same time, publishing a documentation site from this repository ran into two foundational constraints of CASA itself:

1. **Principle 2 (every fact lives in a single file):** maintaining parallel HTML or Markdown pages duplicating the text of the standard, skills, or changelog would create a second source of truth, guaranteed to drift on subsequent PRs.
2. **Zero external dependencies and toolchain isolation:** all reference automation in `casa-standard` runs strictly on the Python 3 standard library; introducing Node/npm, lockfiles, or `pip` packages for a static site generator would pollute the repository tree and must never leak into adopting repositories via `casa-init`.

## Decision Drivers

- **True single source of truth:** the site compiles directly from `STANDARD.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/index.json`, `docs/adr/*.md`, `docs/specs/*.md`, and `docs/templates/skills/*/SKILL.md`; the `_site/` output directory is an ephemeral build artifact ignored by git.
- **Zero external dependencies:** compiler written purely in Python 3 stdlib emitting semantic HTML, vanilla CSS, and vanilla JS — deterministic and testable locally and in CI.
- **Strictly scoped to the reference repository:** `scripts/build-site` and `site/` never enter `casa-init`'s `TOOLCHAIN`, do not alter `docs-check`, and do not change the adopter contract (`casa-version` remains `1.10`, ADR-0010).
- **URL portability:** internal links and asset paths are computed relative to each page's depth, working identically under a GitHub Pages project subpath (`/casa-standard/`), a custom root domain, or a local HTTP server.
- **Explicit visual system and UI states (ADR-0014):** technical-editorial art direction using HSL tokens in CSS custom properties (warm-paper light mode and neutral-charcoal dark mode honoring system preference with a persisted toggle; `Newsreader`, `Plus Jakarta Sans`, and `JetBrains Mono` typography) plus mandatory UI states (search and filter empty-states with a clear-filter action, copy confirmation feedback, and responsive navigation).

## Considered Options

### Option 1 — Hand-written HTML/Markdown pages versioned in `docs/` or `site/`

**Pros:** no build script required.

**Cons:** violates Principle 2 head-on; every edit to `STANDARD.md`, an ADR, or a skill would require manually updating site pages.

### Option 2 — External static site framework (Astro, VitePress, MkDocs, Docusaurus)

**Pros:** off-the-shelf themes and search plugins.

**Cons:** introduces `package.json`/lockfiles or `pip` virtualenvs into a repository premised on running with Python 3 stdlib alone; expands maintenance surface and CI runtime unnecessarily.

### Option 3 — Client-side SPA fetching raw `.md` files in the browser

**Pros:** no HTML build step.

**Cons:** empty HTML without JavaScript, poor SEO/indexing, loading flashes, and brittle relative-path resolution between GitHub Pages subpaths and local previews.

### Option 4 — `scripts/build-site` (Python 3 stdlib) + vanilla assets (`site/`) deployed via `actions/deploy-pages`

**Pros:** static HTML pre-rendered directly from canonical sources; zero external dependencies; deterministic and verifiable via its own test suite (`scripts/test-site`) in the global DoD; official artifact-based GitHub Actions deployment with no `gh-pages` branch polluting git history.

**Cons:** requires maintaining a focused Markdown converter covering the subset used in this repository (headings, lists, GFM tables, blockquotes, fenced code blocks, and inline emphasis).

## Decision

Option 4. Add `scripts/build-site` (Python 3 stdlib) and static presentation assets under `site/` (`style.css`, `app.js`, `favicon.svg`). On every push to `main`, `.github/workflows/pages.yml` compiles `_site/` and publishes to GitHub Pages via `actions/upload-pages-artifact` and `actions/deploy-pages`, with no artifact branch.

`scripts/test-site` joins the global DoD in `AGENTS.md` and `.github/workflows/docs-check.yml`, ensuring that future edits to `STANDARD.md`, ADRs, Specs, or skills never break site compilation or internal links.
